title: Sunset from indoors
hook: a window, a lamp and a pause are enough

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sunset shared, and a three-word invitation. Your line was come and see. Who stood beside you? Day one hundred fifty-two.

This week we watched the sun go: the hour so many traditions mark, the sunset point that walks along the horizon, the colors, and a sunset shared. Lovely, when the sky cooperates. But real life doesn't always. It's raining. It's winter, and the sun sets while you're still at work. Your window faces a brick wall. You're caring for someone and can't step out. Does the ritual just stop? It doesn't have to. People have been marking dusk indoors for as long as there have been indoors. Today's practice is sunset from indoors.
screen: `RAIN, WORK, A BRICK WALL.` → `DOES THE RITUAL STOP?` → `SUNSET FROM INDOORS.`

segments.voice: For most of history, sunset meant one practical thing: light a lamp. And many traditions turned that ordinary moment into something more, each for its own reasons. In the early church, Christians gathered at dusk for the lighting of the lamps, and sang a hymn in Greek called Phos Hilaron, often translated O gladsome light or O joyful light. It's one of the oldest Christian hymns we still have outside the Bible; in the three hundreds, Basil the Great already called it ancient. Orthodox Christians still sing it at vespers today, as the evening light fades. In many Hindu homes, someone lights an oil lamp, a diya, at dusk, often before an image of God, and the evening prayers begin. And as we saw this week, Jewish homes light candles as Shabbat arrives on Friday. Different meanings, different words, different understandings of what the light is. But the gesture is the same one your great-great-grandparents made every evening without thinking: the sky goes dark, so you strike a light. And that's all today's practice needs. A window, even a small one, to notice the light outside changing. A lamp, to turn on by hand at the moment you notice. And a pause, a few breaths long, between the day and the evening. You don't need a horizon. You need to mark the turn. Without a marker, days blur together into one long screen-lit stretch. With one, even a tiny one, the day has an ending. And an ending is what lets the evening begin.
screen: `SUNSET MEANT: LIGHT A LAMP.` · `PHOS HILARON, O GLADSOME LIGHT.` · `A DIYA AT DUSK.` · `A WINDOW, A LAMP, A PAUSE.` · then, large: `THE DAY TURNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse the lamp. Settle, and breathe. Picture the lamp you'll use tonight: a table lamp, a candle if it's safe, the light over the stove. Picture the window nearest it. Tonight, when you notice the light outside fading, you'll go to the lamp and switch it on by hand, slowly, on purpose. Then stand for three breaths. Rehearse it now: reach, switch, breathe. The bell holds the time.
Sunset from indoors. A window, a lamp and a pause: enough to mark the turn from day to evening, whatever the weather. Today's word.
Your line: the day turns. Tonight, at dusk, light one lamp by hand and pause for three breaths. Next week, we build your own routine. Day one hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians sing Phos Hilaron at vespers as the lamps are lit, many Hindu families light a diya at dusk, and Jewish homes light candles as Shabbat begins; many other people simply turn on a lamp and pause.
